title: Astrophysical Journal adopts new guidelines on AI use
content:
Dear Colleague,
The AAS Publications Committee is pleased to share the results of a community request: guidelines for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including large language models, in preparing and reviewing manuscripts submitted to the AAS journals.
Astronomers and planetary scientists are already using AI in many ways, from polishing prose to accelerating code development to assisting with data analysis. Many of you told us, through the AI-use survey we circulated to membership and through direct conversations with the editors, that you wanted clarity on how to use these tools ethically and transparently in your work. The guidelines prepared by the Publications Committee, with input from the editorial board, are intended to address these concerns.
View the AI Guidelines on Our Policy Page
The Publications Committee is a group of working astronomers and planetary scientists — volunteers from across the community who took this on because we care about the integrity of our shared literature. We drafted these guidelines by drawing on current scholarly publishing industry standards and reshaping that guidance around what matters for our authors and fellow astronomers and planetary scientists; the guidelines were informed directly by what you told us in the AI-use survey and from conversations with you as colleagues.
This guidance comes as two companion documents — one for authors and one for reviewers — because the concerns differ for each. As an example, the reviewer guide addresses the confidentiality of unpublished work during peer review, which is its own serious issue. On the author side, the scope covers AI use anywhere while preparing a manuscript for submission — including text, code, and generated figures or images — but not general use of AI in your research more broadly. The guidelines spell out which uses call for a disclosure statement and provide example language you can adapt directly for your specific cases.
These AI guidelines, including a required AI-usage disclosure statement for all submissions, will take effect for new submissions later this fall. We intend these guidelines to be a living document: we expect the landscape around these tools to keep shifting, and we will revisit and update the guidance as it does. If you have a question or feedback, you are welcome to submit it via this form. This document exists because members spoke up the first time; we’d like to keep hearing from you as we go.
Thank you for the trust you place in your journals, and for the effort so many of you already contribute to maintain their value and integrity.
Angela M. Stickle
Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
Chair, AAS Publications Committee

report.summary: AAS journals announce AI usage guidelines for authors and reviewers, effective fall 2025, requiring disclosure statements.
report.background: Astronomers and planetary scientists increasingly use AI tools for writing, coding, and data analysis, prompting concerns about transparency, authorship integrity, and confidentiality. The AAS Publications Committee ran a community survey and consulted editors to understand how members wanted to handle these tools ethically. Drawing on industry publishing standards and adapting them to astronomy-specific needs, the committee produced two companion guidance documents: one for authors and one for reviewers. The author guide covers AI use in preparing manuscripts, including text, code, and figures, while the reviewer guide addresses confidentiality of unpublished work. The guidelines become mandatory for new submissions later this fall, with a required AI-usage disclosure statement. They are intended as a living document to evolve as AI tools change.
key_points: The AAS has created two sets of guidelines: one for authors and one for reviewers, recognizing that the ethical concerns and responsibilities differ between writing and evaluating papers. This split allows tailored advice on issues like confidentiality during peer review versus transparency in manuscript creation.

For authors, the guidelines require an AI-usage disclosure statement for all new submissions starting fall 2025. This covers any use of AI in preparing text, code, or figures, but does not apply to general AI use in broader research activities, keeping the scope focused on the submitted manuscript.

The guidelines were developed from a community survey and direct consultations, reflecting grassroots input from active astronomers and planetary scientists. This approach ensures the rules address real practices and concerns rather than theoretical ones, increasing likely acceptance and compliance within the field.

The AAS explicitly frames the guidance as a living document. Since AI tools and norms are quickly changing, the committee promises to revisit and update the policies periodically, inviting ongoing feedback from members to keep the documents relevant and practical.

The reviewer guide highlights safeguarding the confidentiality of unpublished work during peer review. AI tools that process text externally could leak sensitive research findings, so reviewers are given specific instructions on what uses are acceptable without risking data exposure.
report.impact: This move signals a broader shift in academic publishing: journals are moving from ad hoc reactions to structured AI policies. For the AI industry, it creates clear requirements for how scientific authors may incorporate models into manuscript preparation, likely boosting demand for tools that can log or audit AI contributions for disclosure. Developers need to build transparent provenance features. For researchers and reviewers, the guidelines offer a safe framework for leveraging AI without risking ethics violations or confidentiality breaches. Regular readers gain assurance that paper contributions are transparent, preserving trust in published astronomy research.
report.tools: Researchers can watch for AI-assistance tooling with provenance tracking, such as LangSmith for logging LLM call chains and dataset records, or open-source projects like LangChain and Promptflow for modeling usage. For astronomy-specific workflows, tools like astropy and Jupyter notebooks now need integration with statement generators. The AAS policy also encourages using collaborative writing tools like Overleaf, which may add AI usage declaration templates.
